extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers / American public interested in wartime news
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards about what wartime news and communiqués should disclose or withhold (OWI/censorship practice, handling of communiqués, and how ship losses are reported). Targets journalism and government public-relations practice during active military operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: OWI guiding principle on public right to know
rubrics_metrics.description: "That the American people have right to know everything that would not give him aid if he found out."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OWI's stated guiding principle: release to the public all information that does not aid the enemy. Framed as a broad rule for disclosure decisions during wartime—public has right to know everything not of aid to the enemy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship applies to facts likely to harm the war effort, not to opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Price pointed out his office’s censorship codes do not apply to opinion, but only to facts, information deemed likely to harm the war effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between opinion and factual material when considering suppression. Opinion pieces are not subject to censorship codes; factual reports that could help the enemy are the focus of suppression requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for suppression must not keep the public ignorant
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for suppression must not be so restrictive that they will keep the American people in ignorance of the progress of the war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censors and officials should balance security against the public's need for information; suppression requests should avoid causing widespread distrust or depriving citizens of necessary understanding of war progress. Practical application often involves compromise between public right and protection of men and ships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final judgment on military security rests with professional military officers (with OWI debate)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our office does not claim that anyone but a professional military or naval officer can be the final judge on this question of military security," he said, "but we do claim and exercise the right to debate whether any given question is really a matter of security or only of the ingrained and habitual reticence of the services."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials recognize military professionals as primary judges of security-sensitive information, while civilian agencies (OWI) may debate and question whether secrecy is genuinely security-related or merely habit. Decisions over communiqués may therefore involve consultation with military authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: OWI should not write communiqués; army/navy PR should handle them
rubrics_metrics.description: Davis said OWI was not taking over the writing of communiques because this requires special handling and is best handled by army or navy public relations officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communiqués require coordination of many operational details and therefore should be prepared by the relevant military public-relations offices rather than OWI; OWI's role is complementary rather than replacing service PR apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: OWI's functions abroad: audiences and purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Davis described OWI’s work abroad as aimed at giving news to troops overseas, supplying Allies and neutrals with facts on American war efforts, and convincing enemy nationals that their leaders have insured their ultimate downfall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use overseas information policy both to inform friendly audiences (troops, Allies, neutrals) and to conduct psychological operations aimed at enemy nationals. Tailor releases to these distinct objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic media asked to refrain from spreading harmful news (voluntary cooperation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For domestic news, newspapers and radio stations are asked not to spread harmful news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The government requests voluntary cooperation from domestic press and broadcasters to avoid disseminating information that could harm the war effort; such cooperation is framed as necessary but must be balanced to avoid excessive secrecy or loss of trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting naval/ship losses: categories and disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: The box score of ship losses uses categories: Sunk, Probably sunk, Damaged, and includes footnotes about exclusions: 'Does not include various vessels listed as probably damaged...' and notes where damage to American vessels has not been reported by type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting naval losses, classify reported effects (sunk, probably sunk, damaged) and provide explicit disclaimers about what is and is not included (e.g., probable damages, types not reported). Transparency about reporting limitations and data caveats is part of responsible wartime reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application of OWI policy is complex; Japanese claims often excessive
rubrics_metrics.description: Davis admitted that practical application of the OWI policy was 'not so simple,' since Japanese claims are often 'so excessive,' it is difficult to ascertain what Tokyo actually knows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials must take into account the uncertainty and propaganda in enemy reports when deciding what to release. Over- or under-reacting to enemy claims can complicate disclosure decisions; caution and verification are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between openness and operational security is a frequent compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: The result, he said, is frequently a compromise between the public’s right to know and the need to protect the men and ships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect disclosure decisions to be the outcome of negotiation and compromise between transparency and security—policymakers should document reasoning and seek the least-restrictive suppression consistent with safety.
